paper_b.title: Introduction to the non-asymptotic analysis of random matrices

metadata.description: Paper A (Goodfellow et al.) introduces GANs: a two-player minimax game between a generator and a discriminator neural network, with a JSD-based global-optimum theorem and an SGD training algorithm. Paper B (Vershynin) is a survey of non-asymptotic random matrix theory: singular-value bounds, sub-gaussian/sub-exponential concentration, isotropic random vectors, covariance estimation, and the restricted isometry property. The two papers share no theorems, definitions, proof techniques, or even underlying problem; the only common vocabulary is at the surface level ("matrix", "gradient"). This is a curated negative pair: matches are exclusively `none`.

matches.explanation: Paper A's core definitions (generator network $G$, discriminator network $D$, adversarial value function $V(G,D)$, virtual criterion $C(G)$) define a two-player minimax game between neural networks over data and noise distributions. Paper B has no notion of generator/discriminator, no minimax game, no value function over distributions. Its definitions concern singular values of fixed/random matrices, $\varepsilon$-nets, sub-gaussian/sub-exponential scalar and vector norms, isotropic random vectors, and the restricted isometry constant. Different mathematical universes with no translation.

Paper A's central problem statement and equations express the minimax objective $\min_G\max_D V(D,G)$, the closed form $D^*_G(x)=p_{\text{data}}/(p_{\text{data}}+p_g)$ of the optimal discriminator, and the JSD identity $C(G)=-\log 4 + 2\,\text{JSD}(p_{\text{data}}\|p_g)$. Paper B never sets up an optimization over function-class pairs, never invokes Jensen-Shannon divergence, and has no analogue of an optimal-discriminator formula. No counterpart.

The three named results of paper A (optimal discriminator for fixed $G$; global optimum of $C(G)$ at $p_g=p_{\text{data}}$; non-parametric convergence of Algorithm 1 to the data distribution) are statements about a learning game, proved with calculus + JSD non-negativity + subgradient-of-supremum-of-convex-functions arguments. Paper B's theorems (Gordon's theorem for Gaussian matrices, sub-gaussian/heavy-tailed row & column singular-value bounds, RIP theorems) are deviation/concentration inequalities for random matrices. No theorem-level correspondence.

Paper A's training algorithm is alternating minibatch SGD ($k$ discriminator gradient-ascent steps per generator gradient-descent step). Paper B is a theoretical survey with no algorithm at all -- it states no iterative procedure, no SGD, no training loop. No counterpart.

Paper A's three proofs use (i) pointwise integrand maximization $a\log y + b\log(1-y)$, (ii) algebraic rewriting of $C(G)+\log 4$ as a sum of two KLs and recognizing the JSD identity, and (iii) subgradient calculus for suprema of convex functions. Paper B's proofs are entirely concentration-of-measure arguments: volume covering, Markov+mgf, symmetrization, decoupling, matrix Bernstein. Disjoint proof toolkits.

Paper B's foundational matrix definitions (singular values, spectral norm, $\varepsilon$-nets/covering numbers) underpin all of non-asymptotic random matrix theory. Paper A never defines singular values, never uses the spectral norm of any matrix, and has no $\varepsilon$-net machinery -- its `matrices' are just parameter blobs of MLPs, treated only via gradient updates. No definition-level match.

Sub-gaussian / sub-exponential random variables and their $\psi_2,\psi_1$ norms, isotropic random vectors with $\Sigma=I$, sub-gaussian random vectors via 1-D marginals, and the restricted isometry property are the core probabilistic concepts of paper B. Paper A has no high-dimensional probability vocabulary at all -- only expectations $\mathbb{E}_{p_{\text{data}}}[\cdot]$ and $\mathbb{E}_{p_z}[\cdot]$ inside the value function. No counterpart.

Covering-number bounds for the unit sphere ($(1+2/\varepsilon)^n$) and net-based estimates of the spectral norm (general and symmetric). Paper A has no sphere coverings, no spectral norm of any operator, no net arguments. No match.

Equivalences among sub-gaussian properties (tail / moment / mgf / $\psi_2$ integrability), rotation invariance of sub-gaussians under independent sums, the $X$ sub-gaussian $\Leftrightarrow X^2$ sub-exponential identity, and the centered sub-exponential mgf bound. None of these has any analogue in paper A.

Auxiliary lemmas for paper B: norm/inner-product expectations of isotropic vectors, products of sub-gaussian distributions, the approximate-isometry equivalence ($\|B^*B-I\|$ vs $s_{\min},s_{\max}$ deviation), Banach-space symmetrization with Bernoullis, and the elementary $|Z^2-1|$ vs $|Z-1|$ inequality. Paper A has no analogue of any of these.

Decoupling lemmas (double-array random-subset trick; matrix decoupling for Gram blocks), uniform $|Z^2-1|$-type process inequality, and stochastic-process symmetrization. These technical tools support paper B's heavy-tailed-column and uniform RIP proofs. Paper A has nothing analogous -- no decoupling, no Bernoulli signs, no symmetrization.

Hoeffding-type and Bernstein-type sub-gaussian / sub-exponential large-deviation inequalities for $\sum a_i X_i$, plus Khintchine and average-sub-exponential corollaries. Paper A invokes no concentration inequality; expectations there are over data/noise, not over independent random variables to be controlled in tail. No match.

Rudelson's inequality ($\mathbb{E}\|\sum\varepsilon_i x_i\otimes x_i\|$ bound) and the Gaussian-matrix singular-value deviation bound. These are quintessential random matrix theory results with no analogue in paper A.

Gordon's theorem for Gaussian matrices ($\sqrt N - \sqrt n \le \mathbb{E} s_{\min} \le \mathbb{E} s_{\max} \le \sqrt N + \sqrt n$), and its sub-gaussian-rows / heavy-tailed-rows / non-isotropic-rows extensions. Bedrock random-matrix singular-value bounds. No counterpart in paper A.

Expected-singular-value bounds for heavy-tailed rows / non-isotropic rows / sub-gaussian columns / heavy-tailed columns. All four are random-matrix concentration results requiring symmetrization, Rudelson, and matrix Bernstein. Paper A has no such results.

Sample-complexity bounds for covariance estimation (sub-gaussian and heavy-tailed cases) and frame-subsampling theorems. Paper A has no covariance-estimation problem, no frame, no sub-sampling. No match.

Restricted-isometry-property definition and its sub-gaussian / concentration-implies-RIP / heavy-tailed-uniform / heavy-tailed-RIP theorems -- the compressed-sensing payoff of paper B. Paper A has no RIP, no sparsity, no measurement matrix, no compressed sensing. No counterpart.

Paper B's proofs of the foundational lemmas (volume covering, net-based spectral-norm bound, sub-gaussian equivalences via cyclic implications, rotation-invariance via mgf product, Hoeffding via rotation+tail, Khintchine, sub-exponential-as-square, sub-exponential mgf). All are standard high-dimensional probability arguments -- Markov, Taylor, Hölder. None of these techniques appears in paper A's three proofs.

Proofs of Bernstein for sub-exponentials, isotropic-vector identities, sub-gaussian-marginal product, Rudelson via non-commutative Khintchine, Gordon via Slepian, Gaussian deviation via Lipschitz concentration, and the approximate-isometry equivalence. Pure RMT/concentration toolkit; nothing analogous in paper A.

Proofs of paper B's row-model singular-value bounds: covering+sub-exponential concentration (sub-gaussian rows), matrix Bernstein (heavy-tailed rows isotropic and non-isotropic), symmetrization, $|Z^2-1|$ deviation, and the symmetrization+Rudelson+Cauchy-Schwarz scheme (heavy-tailed expected singular values). No counterpart proof technique in paper A.

Proofs for covariance estimation, sub-frames, decoupling, sub-gaussian-column theorem (covering+decoupling+conditioning), and matrix decoupling + heavy-tailed-column theorem (decoupling+TP9.11+diagonalization). Paper A has no analogue.

Proofs of the RIP theorems: per-subset application of TP9.7/TP9.12 + LP9.11 + union bound, BDDW concentration-implies-RIP, stochastic-process symmetrization, symmetrization+uniform-Rudelson+Cauchy-Schwarz, and the explicit $m\ge\ldots$ rearrangement. Paper A has no RIP, no sparsity, no analogous proof.
